1.summary: Paul praises the God of all comfort who comforts us in affliction so we can comfort others, describes a near-death crisis in Asia, and explains that changing his travel plans wasn't fickleness, since God's promises are all yes in Christ.
1.lookfor: Notice how often the words comfort and affliction appear, and Paul's defense of his honesty.

names.name: Timothy
names.gloss: Paul's co-worker and co-sender.

names.name: Achaia
names.gloss: The Roman province of southern Greece, including Corinth.

names.name: Asia
names.gloss: The Roman province in western Asia Minor, around Ephesus.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: Northern Greece.

names.name: Silvanus
names.gloss: Silas, who helped found the Corinthian church.

insights.title: Comfort
insights.body: Forms of the word comfort, paraklēsis, appear ten times in verses 3 to 7. It means to come alongside and strengthen; the Spirit is called the Paraclete.

insights.title: Comforted to comfort
insights.body: God comforts us in all our affliction so that we may comfort others with the comfort we received (1:4). Suffering becomes a qualification for ministry.

insights.title: Despaired of life
insights.body: In Asia Paul was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired even of life (1:8). We don't know the event, perhaps the riot in Ephesus or an illness. It taught him to rely on the God who raises the dead (1:9).

insights.title: Yes and no
insights.body: Paul had changed his plan to visit, and critics said his word was yes and no at once (1:17). In a culture of honor, an unreliable promise was a serious charge.

insights.title: All God's promises are yes
insights.body: However many God's promises are, in Christ they are yes, and through him we say Amen (1:20). Christ is God's yes to every promise in the Old Testament.

insights.title: The Spirit as a deposit
insights.body: God gave the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment (1:22), the arrabōn, a first installment guaranteeing the rest. It is still the word for an engagement ring in modern Greek.

insights.title: Comfort to pass on
insights.body: Paul says the comfort we receive is meant to be shared. What hard season taught you something you could share with someone going through it now?

2.summary: Paul explains he wrote a tearful letter instead of making another painful visit, urges them to forgive and restore the man who was disciplined, and describes himself as led in Christ's triumph, spreading the fragrance of the knowledge of God.
2.lookfor: Notice Paul's emotion about the earlier letter, and the triumphal procession image.

names.name: Troas
names.gloss: A port in northwest Asia Minor where Paul waited for Titus.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: A Gentile co-worker Paul sent to Corinth.

names.name: Satan
names.gloss: The adversary, who exploits unforgiveness.

insights.title: The tearful letter
insights.body: Paul wrote out of much affliction and anguish of heart, with many tears (2:4). This severe letter is probably lost; some think chapters 10 to 13 preserve part of it.

insights.title: Forgive him now
insights.body: The punishment by the majority is enough; now forgive and comfort him, so he isn't overwhelmed by excessive sorrow (2:6-7). Discipline aims at restoration.

insights.title: Satan's schemes
insights.body: Forgive so that Satan doesn't take advantage of us, for we aren't ignorant of his schemes (2:11). Unforgiveness in the church gives the enemy a foothold.

insights.title: No rest at Troas
insights.body: Even with an open door for the gospel in Troas, Paul had no rest because he didn't find Titus, so he left for Macedonia (2:12-13). He's honest that anxiety for people mattered more than opportunity.

insights.title: The triumph
insights.body: God always leads us in triumph in Christ (2:14). A Roman triumph paraded a victorious general through the city, with incense burning and captives in tow. Paul pictures himself as a captive in Christ's victory parade.

insights.title: Aroma of life and death
insights.body: To some we are the smell of death, to others the fragrance of life (2:16). The same message divides its hearers, as the incense of a triumph meant victory to some and execution to captives.

insights.title: Restoring someone
insights.body: Paul urged the church to welcome back a man who had repented. Is there someone you're keeping at a distance after they've changed?

3.summary: Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter of recommendation, written by the Spirit on hearts; the new covenant of the Spirit outshines the old, and while a veil lies over hearts when Moses is read, turning to the Lord removes it, and we are transformed into his image.
3.lookfor: Notice the contrasts between letter and Spirit, stone and hearts, fading glory and lasting glory.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The lawgiver, whose face shone and who wore a veil.

names.name: Israel
names.gloss: The covenant people at Sinai.

insights.title: Letters of recommendation
insights.body: Travelling teachers carried letters of recommendation from known people (3:1). Paul's rivals had them; Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, known and read by everyone (3:2).

insights.title: Tablets of human hearts
insights.body: The letter is written not on stone tablets but on tablets of flesh, on hearts (3:3), fulfilling the new covenant promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

insights.title: The letter kills
insights.body: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (3:6). The letter here is the law written on stone, holy but powerless to change hearts; it can only condemn.

insights.title: Moses' veil
insights.body: Moses put a veil over his face so Israel wouldn't see the end of the fading glory (3:13). Paul reads Exodus 34 as a picture: the old covenant's glory was real but temporary.

insights.title: Turning to the Lord
insights.body: Whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away (3:16), as Moses removed his veil when he went in to speak with the Lord. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (3:17).

insights.title: From glory to glory
insights.body: We all, with unveiled face, beholding the Lord's glory, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory (3:18). Change comes by looking at Christ.

insights.title: Beholding
insights.body: Paul says we become like what we gaze at. What are you looking at most, and what is it making you into?

4.summary: Paul refuses to distort God's word; the god of this age blinds unbelievers, but God has shone in our hearts; we carry this treasure in clay jars, hard pressed but not crushed, because our light affliction is producing an eternal glory.
4.lookfor: Notice the clay jars image and the paired contrasts in verses 8 and 9.

insights.title: We don't lose heart
insights.body: Paul says twice, we don't lose heart (4:1, 4:16), framing the chapter. His perseverance rests on mercy, not on results.

insights.title: The god of this age
insights.body: Unbelievers are blinded by the god of this world (4:4), Satan, so they can't see the light of the gospel. Paul's job is to proclaim Jesus as Lord, not himself.

insights.title: Let light shine
insights.body: The God who said light shall shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts (4:6). Paul ties conversion to creation's first day: a new creation begins with light.

insights.title: Clay jars
insights.body: We have this treasure in clay jars (4:7). Cheap pottery was the throwaway container of the ancient world, sometimes used to hide valuables. The weakness of the jar shows the power belongs to God.

insights.title: But not
insights.body: Pressed on every side, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; pursued, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed (4:8-9). Each phrase admits the pain and denies the defeat.

insights.title: Light affliction
insights.body: Our light, momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison (4:17). Paul, who was beaten and shipwrecked, calls it light only in comparison with what's coming.

insights.title: What is unseen
insights.body: Paul looks not at what is seen, which is temporary, but at what is unseen, which is eternal (4:18). What would change if you looked at your trouble that way today?

5.summary: Paul longs for the resurrection body, our heavenly dwelling, and walks by faith; Christ's love compels him, since anyone in Christ is a new creation, and God has given him the ministry of reconciliation, pleading with people to be reconciled to God.
5.lookfor: Notice the tent and building images, and the central verse on the exchange in verse 21.

insights.title: A tent
insights.body: Our earthly house is a tent (5:1). Paul the tentmaker knew tents were temporary shelters; God's building is permanent.

insights.title: By faith, not sight
insights.body: We walk by faith, not by sight (5:7). Paul would rather be at home with the Lord, but either way his aim is to please him (5:8-9).

insights.title: The love of Christ compels
insights.body: The love of Christ compels us (5:14). The verb means to hold together or press in on all sides: Christ's death for all leaves Paul no other way to live.

insights.title: A new creation
insights.body: If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old has passed away, the new has come (5:17). Paul speaks of more than personal change: God's new world has broken in.

insights.title: Reconciliation
insights.body: God reconciled us to himself through Christ (5:18). Reconcile, katallassō, was used for restoring a broken relationship, like enemies or estranged spouses. God took the first step.

insights.title: The great exchange
insights.body: God made him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become God's righteousness (5:21). Isaiah's servant bore the sins of many.

insights.title: Ambassadors
insights.body: Paul calls believers ambassadors, as though God were pleading through them (5:20). Who might God be asking you to represent him to?

6.summary: Paul urges them not to receive God's grace in vain, since now is the day of salvation; he lists his hardships and integrity as proof of his ministry, opens his heart wide to them, and warns them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers.
6.lookfor: Notice the long list of paradoxes in verses 8 to 10 and Paul's plea for open hearts.

names.name: Belial
names.gloss: A name for Satan, from a Hebrew word meaning worthlessness.

insights.title: Now is the day
insights.body: Paul quotes Isaiah: in an acceptable time I listened to you, and adds, now is the day of salvation (6:2). The promised time of favor has arrived.

insights.title: Through all things
insights.body: Paul's list moves from hardships (beatings, imprisonments, riots) to virtues (purity, kindness, love) to paradoxes (6:4-10). His life is his credentials.

insights.title: Having nothing
insights.body: As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing all things (6:10). The world sees loss; faith sees wealth.

insights.title: Open your hearts
insights.body: Our heart is wide open to you; you're not restricted by us but by your own affections (6:11-12). Paul's love was not the problem; their coldness was.

insights.title: Unequally yoked
insights.body: Don't be unequally yoked with unbelievers (6:14). The law forbade plowing with an ox and a donkey together; mismatched animals pull in different directions.

insights.title: I will dwell among them
insights.body: Paul strings together promises: I will live in them and walk among them, and be their God (6:16-18), from Leviticus, Isaiah and 2 Samuel. God's people are his temple.

insights.title: Partnerships
insights.body: Paul warned against partnerships that pull you away from God. Is there a relationship or commitment pulling you in a direction you don't want to go?

7.summary: Paul urges them to make room in their hearts, describes his joy when Titus arrived with news of their repentance, and explains that his severe letter caused godly sorrow that led to repentance, not regret.
7.lookfor: Notice the difference between godly sorrow and worldly sorrow, and Paul's relief.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: The co-worker who brought Paul good news from Corinth.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: Where Paul was waiting, troubled on every side.

insights.title: Fights without, fears within
insights.body: In Macedonia Paul had no rest: conflicts on the outside, fears within (7:5). Even apostles feel fear.

insights.title: God comforts the downcast
insights.body: God, who comforts the lowly, comforted us by the coming of Titus (7:6). God's comfort came through a friend's arrival and good news.

insights.title: Godly sorrow
insights.body: Godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, without regret; worldly sorrow produces death (7:10). One turns toward God, the other only feels bad about consequences.

insights.title: No regret
insights.body: Paul says he doesn't regret the painful letter, though he did for a while (7:8). Love sometimes hurts in order to heal.

insights.title: Earnestness
insights.body: Their sorrow produced earnestness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and vindication (7:11). In an honor culture, publicly reversing course took courage.

insights.title: Reconciled
insights.body: Paul rejoices that he has complete confidence in them (7:16). The first seven chapters move from pain to restored relationship, a model of reconciliation in practice.

insights.title: Two kinds of sorrow
insights.body: Paul distinguished sorrow that leads to change from sorrow that only leads to despair. When you've done wrong, which kind do you tend toward?

8.summary: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, points to Christ who became poor to make us rich, urges the Corinthians to finish the collection they began, and explains how Titus and others will handle the money honestly.
8.lookfor: Notice where the Macedonians' generosity came from, and the care Paul takes with financial accountability.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: Northern Greece, whose churches were poor but generous.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: Paul's co-worker, sent to complete the collection.

insights.title: Deep poverty, rich generosity
insights.body: The Macedonian churches, in great affliction and deep poverty, overflowed in generosity, giving beyond their ability and begging to take part (8:2-4).

insights.title: First themselves
insights.body: They gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us (8:5). Generosity with money flowed from surrender of self.

insights.title: He became poor
insights.body: You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for your sakes, so that through his poverty you might become rich (8:9). Giving is grace imitating grace.

insights.title: No lack
insights.body: Paul quotes the manna story: whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack (8:15). The goal is equality, not burden.

insights.title: Handling money honestly
insights.body: Paul sends Titus with a brother chosen by the churches to avoid any blame in handling this large gift, taking care to do what is honorable before the Lord and people (8:20-21). Charges of profiteering were common against travelling teachers.

insights.title: Grace
insights.body: Paul calls the collection a grace, charis, repeatedly in this chapter (8:1, 8:6, 8:7, 8:9). Giving isn't a tax; it's a gift of God working through people.

insights.title: Beyond ability
insights.body: The poorest church gave the most freely. What holds you back from generosity: lack, or fear?

9.summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to have their gift ready before he arrives, teaches that whoever sows generously will reap generously, that God loves a cheerful giver and will supply their needs, and that their giving will cause many to thank God.
9.lookfor: Notice the sowing and reaping image, and how giving leads to thanksgiving.

names.name: Macedonia
names.gloss: Northern Greece, whose believers had heard Paul boast about Corinth.

names.name: Achaia
names.gloss: Southern Greece, where Corinth was.

insights.title: Don't embarrass me
insights.body: Paul had boasted to the Macedonians about Corinth's eagerness, and doesn't want to be embarrassed if they arrive and find the Corinthians unprepared (9:3-4). A very human moment.

insights.title: Sowing and reaping
insights.body: Whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will reap bountifully (9:6). Proverbs says the generous will be enriched.

insights.title: A cheerful giver
insights.body: God loves a cheerful giver (9:7). The Greek word is hilaros, the root of hilarious: glad, ready, not grudging.

insights.title: Enough to share
insights.body: God is able to make all grace abound, so that you always have enough of everything and abound in every good work (9:8). He provides not for hoarding but so we can give.

insights.title: Thanksgiving to God
insights.body: The gift supplies the saints' needs and overflows in many thanksgivings to God (9:12). It also binds Gentile and Jewish believers together in prayer for each other (9:14).

insights.title: Indescribable gift
insights.body: Paul ends: thanks be to God for his indescribable gift (9:15). After two chapters about money, he points to the gift no one can match.

insights.title: Cheerful
insights.body: Paul says each should give what they've decided in their heart, not under pressure. Does your giving feel glad or reluctant?

10.summary: Paul answers those who say he is bold in letters but weak in person; he fights with spiritual weapons that demolish strongholds, refuses to compare himself with others, and boasts only in the Lord within the field God assigned him.
10.lookfor: Notice the change of tone from the earlier chapters, and the military images.

insights.title: A change of tone
insights.body: Chapters 10 to 13 turn sharp and defensive. Perhaps new trouble arose after Paul wrote 1 to 9, or he is now addressing a minority still siding with his rivals.

insights.title: Meek and gentle
insights.body: Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (10:1). His opponents mocked him as humble in person; he says humility is Christ's own way.

insights.title: Strongholds
insights.body: Our weapons are mighty before God to demolish strongholds (10:4), the language of siege warfare. The strongholds are arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God.

insights.title: Every thought captive
insights.body: We take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ (10:5). Thoughts are treated like prisoners of war, brought under Christ's rule.

insights.title: Weak in presence
insights.body: His critics say his letters are weighty but his bodily presence is weak and his speech despicable (10:10). Greek audiences prized polished speakers with commanding presence.

insights.title: Boast in the Lord
insights.body: Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord (10:17), quoting Jeremiah, as in 1 Corinthians. What counts is the Lord's commendation, not self-commendation.

insights.title: Comparing
insights.body: Paul says those who measure themselves by each other are without understanding (10:12). Where do you tend to measure yourself against others?

11.summary: Paul fears the Corinthians are being led astray by super-apostles who preach another Jesus; he defends preaching free of charge, exposes the rivals as false apostles disguised as servants of righteousness, and reluctantly boasts of his sufferings.
11.lookfor: Notice the bride image at the start, and how Paul boasts of the very things others would hide.

names.name: Eve
names.gloss: The first woman, deceived by the serpent.

names.name: Hebrews
names.gloss: Jews, especially Aramaic-speaking ones.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: The Syrian city Paul escaped from.

names.name: Aretas
names.gloss: Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans, whose governor tried to seize Paul.

insights.title: A pure bride
insights.body: Paul promised them as a pure virgin to one husband, Christ, and fears that, as the serpent deceived Eve, their minds will be led away from simple devotion (11:2-3).

insights.title: Super-apostles
insights.body: Paul sarcastically calls his rivals the very chiefest apostles, or super-apostles (11:5). They boasted of credentials, eloquence and Jewish pedigree.

insights.title: Why Paul worked for free
insights.body: Paul preached without charge so as not to be a burden (11:7-9). In Corinth, a paid teacher became a client of his patrons; by refusing, Paul stayed free, but some took it as an insult.

insights.title: An angel of light
insights.body: Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, so his servants pose as servants of righteousness (11:14-15). Deception rarely looks dark.

insights.title: The catalogue
insights.body: Five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and day in the sea (11:24-25). Acts records only some of these.

insights.title: Boasting in weakness
insights.body: If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness (11:30). Paul's climactic example is being lowered in a basket out of Damascus (11:32-33), the opposite of a hero's wall-climbing.

insights.title: Care for the churches
insights.body: Beyond all his sufferings, Paul names the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches (11:28). Whose burdens do you carry in prayer?

12.summary: Paul tells of a man caught up to paradise fourteen years earlier, then of a thorn in the flesh that God refused to remove, saying my grace is sufficient; he defends his apostolic signs and fears what he will find on his third visit.
12.lookfor: Notice that Paul speaks of his vision in the third person, and the answer he received to his prayer.

names.name: Satan
names.gloss: The adversary, whose messenger tormented Paul.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: Paul's co-worker, who didn't exploit the Corinthians.

insights.title: I know a man
insights.body: Paul knows a man caught up to the third heaven, into paradise (12:2-4). He speaks of himself in the third person, uneasy about boasting of visions as his rivals did.

insights.title: The third heaven
insights.body: Jewish writers spoke of layered heavens: the sky, the stars, then God's dwelling. The third heaven means God's very presence.

insights.title: The thorn in the flesh
insights.body: A thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, was given to keep Paul from being proud (12:7). Guesses include an eye disease, recurring illness or persistent opponents; Paul doesn't say, which lets every reader find themselves here.

insights.title: Three times
insights.body: Paul begged the Lord three times to remove it (12:8). Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane for the cup to pass, and accepted the Father's answer.

insights.title: Power made perfect in weakness
insights.body: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (12:9). The theme of the whole letter: when I am weak, then I am strong (12:10).

insights.title: A parent's heart
insights.body: Paul won't be a burden; children shouldn't save up for parents, but parents for children (12:14). He will gladly spend and be spent for them, even if loved less (12:15).

insights.title: Unanswered prayer
insights.body: God answered Paul's prayer, but not with a yes. Is there a weakness God may be using rather than removing?

13.summary: Paul warns that on his third visit he will not spare those who persist in sin, urges them to examine themselves, prays for their restoration, and closes with an appeal for unity and the Trinitarian blessing.
13.lookfor: Notice Paul's call to self-examination and the final blessing naming Father, Son and Spirit.

insights.title: Two or three witnesses
insights.body: Every matter will be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses (13:1), from the law. Paul's visits serve as witnesses.

insights.title: Crucified in weakness
insights.body: Christ was crucified through weakness, yet lives by God's power; we too are weak in him but will live with him by God's power (13:4). Paul's weakness follows Jesus' pattern.

insights.title: Examine yourselves
insights.body: They demanded proof that Christ spoke through Paul; he turns it around: examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith (13:5).

insights.title: Be perfected
insights.body: Paul prays for their perfecting (13:9), katartisis, used of mending nets or setting bones. He wants them restored, not punished.

insights.title: A holy kiss
insights.body: Greet one another with a holy kiss (13:12). A kiss on the cheek was a family greeting; using it among believers of every class declared them one family.

insights.title: The grace
insights.body: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all (13:14). This blessing, used in churches ever since, names Father, Son and Spirit together.

insights.title: Self-examination
insights.body: Paul urged his critics to look at their own hearts. What would honest self-examination show you today?

intro.who: Paul wrote it, with Timothy (1:1), to the church in Corinth. It is his most personal letter.
intro.when: About AD 55–56, from Macedonia, after a painful visit and a severe letter, when Titus brought news that many Corinthians had repented (7:5-7).
intro.why: To express relief and reconciliation, to explain his changed travel plans, to urge generosity in the collection for Jerusalem, and to defend his ministry against rival super-apostles who mocked his weakness. Its great theme is God's power made perfect in weakness.

outline.title: The ministry of the new covenant
